::: {.team-note}
## Summary {.unlisted}
This page covers the choice between primary and secondary data, how to assess what administrative sources already exist and whether they contain the right outcomes, where to find secondary firm-level data, and how to set up data-sharing agreements.
:::


With the Theory of Change (ToC), learning questions, indicators in place, and the feasibility of the randomised controlled trial (RCT) confirmed, the next question is where the data will come from. This is a strategic decision that must be made before the programme launches - not an operational detail to be worked out later. Getting it wrong wastes resources, delays the evaluation, or produces data that cannot support the intended analysis.

---

## The fundamental decision: primary, secondary, or both?

For each indicator in your evaluation framework, you must decide whether to rely on **primary data** collected specifically for the evaluation, **secondary data** that already exists in administrative records, or a **combination of both**.

**Primary data** is information collected directly from target respondents - firms, individuals, or organisations - through surveys or interviews. It gives you control over exactly what is measured and can capture outcomes and mechanisms that administrative records do not contain. The trade-off is cost, time, and respondent burden.

**Secondary data** draws on records that already exist - national business registries, tax authority data, customs records, patent office databases, or the programme's own management information system. It is generally cheaper, covers larger samples, and often provides years of pre-intervention history that is invaluable for establishing baselines. The trade-off is that it may not contain the specific variables you need, and access can take time to negotiate.

In countries where administrative data sources - such as business registries, tax records, and social security data - are well established and reliable, as is generally the case across the European Union, combining both sources is often the most effective approach: secondary data provides broad coverage and pre-intervention history, while primary survey data captures the outcomes and mechanisms that administrative records cannot.

::: {.example .romania}
[North-East Romania: data sources]{.tag}

North-East Romania used a combination of primary and secondary data: self-reported survey data was collected using a structured questionnaire that complements administrative data sources. 
:::

### Comparison of primary vs. secondary data {.unlisted}

| Topic | Primary data | Secondary data (administrative) |
|---|---|---|
| Reporting bias | Less subject to reporting bias | May be subject to reporting bias |
| Sample size | Smaller | Larger |
| Timeliness | Collected when needed | Often published with a delay |
| Cost | More expensive | Cheaper |
| Relevance | Tailored precisely to the outcome of interest | General purpose |
| Pre-intervention history | Limited | History of pre-intervention data available |
| Depth | Richer understanding of mechanisms | Less granular |
| Long-term impacts | Harder to capture | Measuring longer-term impacts is possible |
| Access | Generally straightforward | May require data-sharing agreements |
| Privacy | Can be anonymised | Personal data may not be anonymised |

## Assess what you already have

Before commissioning a new survey, take stock of the administrative data you already hold or can access. Programme management systems typically record beneficiary characteristics, grant amounts, payment dates, and reported output indicators. National statistical offices, tax authorities, business registries, and customs agencies hold firm-level data on turnover, employment, exports, costs, expenditures and tax payments - often going back many years, which is particularly valuable for establishing pre-intervention baselines.

Two questions determine whether administrative sources can be useful for an evaluation. 

First, do they contain the right outcomes? Administrative records capture variables that may or may not align with the outcomes the evaluation is designed to measure. An innovation programme that wants to measure R&D expenditure or product novelty will find that some business registries simply do not record these. Before relying on administrative data, map each indicator in your evaluation framework against what each source actually contains, and identify the gaps.

Second, can the administrative data be linked to the companies being part of the evaluation? If a firm's VAT number or national registration number is collected at application stage, it can serve as a linking key to match programme records against tax, registry, or customs data - enabling outcome measurement without any additional burden on firms. Where no common identifier exists, linkage may still be possible through name and address matching, but this requires more effort and introduces matching errors.

## Where to find secondary firm-level data

Key sources of secondary firm-level data

| Source | What it contains | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National business registry | Firm registration, legal form, ownership, sector (NACE), address | Usually public or via national statistical office |
| Tax authority records | Turnover, VAT declarations, corporate tax filings, payroll | Via data-sharing agreement with tax authority |
| Social security records | Employment headcount, wage bill, employee characteristics | Via data-sharing agreement with social security body |
| Orbis (Bureau van Dijk) | Financial statements, ownership, M&A activity - 400m+ firms globally | Commercial licence required |
| National commercial data providers | Private companies aggregating and selling access to firm-level data compiled from business registries, court records, and financial filings | Via Internet |
| National R&D surveys | R&D expenditure, personnel, outputs - linked to Frascati Manual | Via national statistical office |
| Programme management system | Beneficiary list, grant amounts, disbursement dates, output indicators | Held internally by the Managing Authority |


::: {.example .romania}
[North-East Romania: administrative data]{.tag}

North-East Romania used two administrative data sources: (i) publicly available financial records from the Romanian Ministry of Finance, which contain information on annual revenues, profits, and firm size and (ii) the ORBIS database.
:::

## Data-sharing agreements

Access to administrative data rarely happens automatically. Tax records, social security data, and business registry microdata are typically held by separate government bodies and subject to their own access rules. Negotiating access takes time - in some countries, many months - and must be initiated well before the evaluation begins.

A data-sharing agreement between the Managing Authority and the data-holding body should specify: what data will be shared; in what format and at what level of disaggregation; under what conditions it may be used; who is responsible for data security; and how long it will be retained. General Data Protection Regulation compliance must be addressed explicitly in the agreement.
